newsitem.title: USA: Nevada Power seeks to issue bonds for QFs.
newsitem.headline: Nevada Power seeks to issue bonds for QFs.

text.p: Nevada Power Co said Tuesday it supports proposed state legislation to allow public electric utilities in Nevada the option to issue bonds for the sole purpose of lowering the cost of power purchased under Qualifying Facilities (QF) contracts.

Early last week, Senator Randolph Townsend, chairman of the Nevada Senate Commerce and Labor Committee and a leader in the electricity restructuring debate, said the requested legislation would not pass without a divestiture of Nevada Power's assets, the utility noted.

But Nevada Power said in a statement it "will not consent to a forced divestiture of its assets now or in the future. While Senator Townsend's statements are obviously disappointing, the company expects that the proposal will receive a fair hearing on its merits," said Charles Lenzie, the utility's chairman.
A QF is a non-utility cogeneration facility, or a small power production facility that has met certain federal operating requirements.
Utilities like Nevada Power are required by a 1978 federal law to enter into purchased power agreements with QFs.
Prices in these QF contracts are considered high by today's purchased power market standards, and those costs are are currently being recovered from customers.
In 1996, QFs provided less than 20 percent of Nevada Power's power, yet accounted for 40 percent of total fuel and purchased power costs, the utility said.

The financing mechanism proposed by the legislation would provide utilities with an alternative means of financing a buy-down or buy-out of the contracts and is similar to asset backed securitization mechanisms already adopted in several states, including Washington, Pennsylvania and California.
Nevada Power said it has retained Credit Suisse First Boston as its advisor with respect to the proposed legislation.
